cultures.name: Babylonian (Mesopotamia)
cultures.people: Babylonians and Assyrians; the month names live on in the Hebrew and Levantine calendars
cultures.overview: A lunisolar calendar: each month began when the new crescent was first seen at sunset. Scholars at court kept hemerologies, lists of days favourable or unfavourable for particular activities.

systems.name: Babylonian lunisolar calendar
systems.description: Twelve lunar months, with an extra month inserted when needed to keep the year in step with the seasons.
systems.month_rule: Each month began when a new crescent moon was first sighted low on the western horizon at sunset. A month had 29 or 30 days.
systems.year_rule: The year began with Nisānu, in spring. The first day of the first month could be up to about 20 days from the spring equinox.
systems.intercalation: An extra month (usually a second Addaru) was inserted, at first by decree and later by the 19-year Metonic cycle.
systems.uncertainty: Weather could delay the sighting of the crescent, and in the Neo-Assyrian period the start of a month was sometimes shifted back a day afterwards.

months.name: Nisānu
months.translation: Month [the proxies of the gods are] placed beside the throne
months.description: The Sumerian name means "Month [the proxies of the gods are] placed beside the throne".
months.uncertainty: Gregorian equivalents are rough: the month followed the Moon, and the year was kept near the seasons by inserting an extra month.

lunar_days.name: First crescent
lunar_days.meaning: A new month began on the evening the new crescent was first sighted low in the west at sunset.
lunar_days.uncertainty: Hemerologies varied between copies, months and periods; this is a general pattern, not a rule for every month. Modern dates come from an illustrative model of the Babylonian month (first crescent seen in Babylon), not an ancient listing.

lunar_days.name: Day 7
lunar_days.meaning: One of the days that fell on the Moon's phases (7th, 14th, 21st, 28th), which seem to have been systematically unfavourable. Offerings were made to Marduk and Ishtar, apparently at nightfall.
lunar_days.uncertainty: Hemerologies varied between copies, months and periods; this is a general pattern, not a rule for every month. Modern dates come from an illustrative model of the Babylonian month (first crescent seen in Babylon), not an ancient listing.

lunar_days.name: Day 14
lunar_days.meaning: One of the days that fell on the Moon's phases (7th, 14th, 21st, 28th), which seem to have been systematically unfavourable. Offerings were made to Ninlil and Nergal, apparently at nightfall.
lunar_days.uncertainty: Hemerologies varied between copies, months and periods; this is a general pattern, not a rule for every month. Modern dates come from an illustrative model of the Babylonian month (first crescent seen in Babylon), not an ancient listing.

lunar_days.name: Day 21
lunar_days.meaning: One of the days that fell on the Moon's phases (7th, 14th, 21st, 28th), which seem to have been systematically unfavourable. Offerings were made to Sin and Shamash, apparently at nightfall.
lunar_days.uncertainty: Hemerologies varied between copies, months and periods; this is a general pattern, not a rule for every month. Modern dates come from an illustrative model of the Babylonian month (first crescent seen in Babylon), not an ancient listing.

lunar_days.name: Day 28
lunar_days.meaning: One of the days that fell on the Moon's phases (7th, 14th, 21st, 28th), which seem to have been systematically unfavourable. Offerings were made to Enki and Mah, apparently at nightfall. At least the 28th was known as a rest day.
lunar_days.uncertainty: Hemerologies varied between copies, months and periods; this is a general pattern, not a rule for every month. Modern dates come from an illustrative model of the Babylonian month (first crescent seen in Babylon), not an ancient listing.

lunar_days.name: Šapattu (full Moon)
lunar_days.meaning: The full-Moon day, šapattu: "day of mid-repose" (ūm nūḫ libbi), in the middle of the month.
lunar_days.uncertainty: Hemerologies varied between copies, months and periods; this is a general pattern, not a rule for every month. Modern dates come from an illustrative model of the Babylonian month (first crescent seen in Babylon), not an ancient listing.

lunar_days.name: Day 19
lunar_days.meaning: Listed with the 7th, 14th, 21st and 28th as a day of abstinence in the month Ulūlu (Elul). Older scholarship notes it is the 49th day (7 × 7) from the start of the previous month.
lunar_days.uncertainty: 1906 scholarship for one month (Ulūlu); not every month. Illustrative modern date.

observances.name: No fish or leeks
observances.description: Nisānu, day 2: fish and leeks should not be eaten.
observances.uncertainty: From one hemerology as summarised by the University of Hamburg's CSMC. Applies to this one month of the Babylonian year; the modern date is an illustrative reconstruction.

observances.name: No fish or leeks; a day to marry

observances.uncertainty: From one hemerology as summarised by the University of Hamburg's CSMC. Applies to this one month of the Babylonian year; the modern date is an illustrative reconstruction.

recommendations.historical_practice: An "evil day" (unsuitable for prohibited activities): officials were barred from various activities and ordinary people were forbidden to "make a wish"; offerings to Marduk and Ishtar.
recommendations.uncertainty: Hemerologies varied between copies, months and periods; this is a general pattern, not a rule for every month. Modern dates come from an illustrative model of the Babylonian month (first crescent seen in Babylon), not an ancient listing.
recommendations.modern_interpretation: Treat it as a quiet day: hold back from big decisions or new undertakings (modern suggestion).
